1679 class MatrixDeterminant(MatrixArithmetic, MatrixOperations, MatrixShaping):
1680     """Provides basic matrix determinant operations.
1681     Should not be instantiated directly."""
1682 
1683     def _eval_berkowitz_toeplitz_matrix(self):
1684         """Return (A,T) where T the Toeplitz matrix used in the Berkowitz algorithm
1685         corresponding to `self` and A is the first principal submatrix."""
1686 
1687         # the 0 x 0 case is trivial
1688         if self.rows == 0 and self.cols == 0:
1689             return self._new(1,1, [S.One])
1690 
1691         #
1692         # Partition self = [ a_11  R ]
1693         #                  [ C     A ]
1694         #
1695 
1696         a, R = self[0,0],   self[0, 1:]
1697         C, A = self[1:, 0], self[1:,1:]
1698 
1699         #
1700         # The Toeplitz matrix looks like
1701         #
1702         #  [ 1                                     ]
1703         #  [ -a         1                          ]
1704         #  [ -RC       -a        1                 ]
1705         #  [ -RAC     -RC       -a       1         ]
1706         #  [ -RA**2C -RAC      -RC      -a       1 ]
1707         #  etc.
1708 
1709         # Compute the diagonal entries.
1710         # Because multiplying matrix times vector is so much
1711         # more efficient than matrix times matrix, recursively
1712         # compute -R * A**n * C.
1713         diags = [C]
1714         for i in range(self.rows - 2):
1715             diags.append(A * diags[i])
1716         diags = [(-R*d)[0, 0] for d in diags]
1717         diags = [S.One, -a] + diags
1718 
1719         def entry(i,j):
1720             if j > i:
1721                 return S.Zero
1722             return diags[i - j]
1723 
1724         toeplitz = self._new(self.cols + 1, self.rows, entry)
1725         return (A, toeplitz)
1726 
1727     def _eval_berkowitz_vector(self):
1728         """ Run the Berkowitz algorithm and return a vector whose entries
1729             are the coefficients of the characteristic polynomial of `self`.
1730 
1731             Given N x N matrix, efficiently compute
1732             coefficients of characteristic polynomials of 'self'
1733             without division in the ground domain.
1734 
1735             This method is particularly useful for computing determinant,
1736             principal minors and characteristic polynomial when 'self'
1737             has complicated coefficients e.g. polynomials. Semi-direct
1738             usage of this algorithm is also important in computing
1739             efficiently sub-resultant PRS.
1740 
1741             Assuming that M is a square matrix of dimension N x N and
1742             I is N x N identity matrix, then the Berkowitz vector is
1743             an N x 1 vector whose entries are coefficients of the
1744             polynomial
1745 
1746                            charpoly(M) = det(t*I - M)
1747 
1748             As a consequence, all polynomials generated by Berkowitz
1749             algorithm are monic.
1750 
1751            For more information on the implemented algorithm refer to:
1752 
1753            [1] S.J. Berkowitz, On computing the determinant in small
1754                parallel time using a small number of processors, ACM,
1755                Information Processing Letters 18, 1984, pp. 147-150
1756 
1757            [2] M. Keber, Division-Free computation of sub-resultants
1758                using Bezout matrices, Tech. Report MPI-I-2006-1-006,
1759                Saarbrucken, 2006
1760         """
1761 
1762         # handle the trivial cases
1763         if self.rows == 0 and self.cols == 0:
1764             return self._new(1, 1, [S.One])
1765         elif self.rows == 1 and self.cols == 1:
1766             return self._new(2, 1, [S.One, -self[0,0]])
1767 
1768         submat, toeplitz = self._eval_berkowitz_toeplitz_matrix()
1769         return toeplitz * submat._eval_berkowitz_vector()
1770 
1771     def _eval_det_bareiss(self):
1772         """Compute matrix determinant using Bareiss' fraction-free
1773         algorithm which is an extension of the well known Gaussian
1774         elimination method. This approach is best suited for dense
1775         symbolic matrices and will result in a determinant with
1776         minimal number of fractions. It means that less term
1777         rewriting is needed on resulting formulae.
1778 
1779         TODO: Implement algorithm for sparse matrices (SFF),
1780         http://www.eecis.udel.edu/~saunders/papers/sffge/it5.ps.
1781         """
1782 
1783         # XXX included as a workaround for issue #12362.  Should use `_find_reasonable_pivot` instead
1784         def _find_pivot(l):
1785             for pos,val in enumerate(l):
1786                 if val:
1787                     return (pos, val, None, None)
1788             return (None, None, None, None)

1791         # Recursively implimented Bareiss' algorithm as per Deanna Richelle Leggett's
1792         # thesis http://www.math.usm.edu/perry/Research/Thesis_DRL.pdf
1793         def bareiss(mat, cumm=1):
1794             if mat.rows == 0:
1795                 return S.One
1796             elif mat.rows == 1:
1797                 return mat[0, 0]
1798 
1799             # find a pivot and extract the remaining matrix
1800             # XXX should use `_find_reasonable_pivot`.  Blocked by issue #12362
1801             pivot_pos, pivot_val, _, _ = _find_pivot(mat[:, 0])
1802             if pivot_pos == None:
1803                 return S.Zero
1804 
1805             # if we have a valid pivot, we'll do a "row swap", so keep the
1806             # sign of the det
1807             sign = (-1) ** (pivot_pos % 2)
1808 
1809             # we want every row but the pivot row and every column
1810             rows = list(i for i in range(mat.rows) if i != pivot_pos)
1811             cols = list(range(mat.cols))
1812             tmp_mat = mat.extract(rows, cols)
1813 
1814             def entry(i, j):
1815                 ret = (pivot_val*tmp_mat[i, j + 1] - mat[pivot_pos, j + 1]*tmp_mat[i, 0]) / cumm
1816                 if not ret.is_Atom:
1817                     cancel(ret)
1818                 return ret
1819 
1820             return sign*bareiss(self._new(mat.rows - 1, mat.cols - 1, entry), pivot_val)
1821 
1822         return cancel(bareiss(self))

1829     def _eval_det_lu(self):
1830         """ Use LU the decomposition to compute the determinant."""
1831         try:
1832             l, u, p = self.LUdecomposition()
1833         except ValueError:
1834             # if there is a value error in the LU decomposition, it means the matrix
1835             # wasn't invertible
1836             return S.Zero

1839         det = (-1) ** (len(p) % 2)
1840         # multiply by the diagonal entries
1841         for k in range(self.rows):

1844         return det

1861     def charpoly(self, x=Dummy('lambda'), simplify=_simplify):
1862         """Computes characteristic polynomial det(x*I - self) where I is
1863         the identity matrix.
1864 
1865         A PurePoly is returned, so using different variables for ``x`` does
1866         not affect the comparison or the polynomials:

1869         ========

1872         >>> from sympy.abc import x, y

1874         >>> A.charpoly(x) == A.charpoly(y)

1878         default (which looks good when pretty-printed in unicode):

1884         symbol, so using the default (``lambda``) or your own Dummy symbol is
1885         the safest option:

1887         >>> A = Matrix([[1, 2], [x, 0]])
1888         >>> A.charpoly().as_expr()
1889         _lambda**2 - _lambda - 2*x
1890         >>> A.charpoly(x).as_expr()

1897         the characteristic polynomial efficiently and without any
1898         division operations.  Thus the characteristic polynomial over any
1899         commutative ring without zero divisors can be computed.

1902         ========

1943     def det(self, method="bareiss"):
1944         """Computes the determinant of a matrix.  If the matrix
1945         is at most 3x3, a hard-coded formula is used.
1946         Otherwise, the determinant using the method `method`.
1947 
1948 
1949         Possible values for "method":
1950           bareis
1951           berkowitz
1952           lu
1953         """
1954 
1955         # sanitize `method`
1956         method = method.lower()
1957         if method == "bareis":
1958             SymPyDeprecationWarning(
1959                 feature="Using 'bareis' to compute matrix determinant",
1960                 useinstead="'bareiss'",
1961                 issue=12363, deprecated_since_version="1.1").warn()
1962             method = "bareiss"
1963         if method == "det_lu":
1964             SymPyDeprecationWarning(
1965                 feature="Using 'det_lu' to compute matrix determinant",
1966                 useinstead="'lu'",
1967                 deprecated_since_version="1.1").warn()
1968             method = "lu"
1969         if method not in ("bareiss", "berkowitz", "lu"):
1970             raise ValueError("Determinant method '%s' unrecognized" % method)
1971 
1972         # if methods were made internal and all determinant calculations
1973         # passed through here, then these lines could be factored out of
1974         # the method routines
1975         if self.rows != self.cols:
1976             raise NonSquareMatrixError()
1977 
1978         n = self.rows
1979         if n == 0:
1980             return S.One
1981         elif n == 1:
1982             return self[0,0]
1983         elif n == 2:
1984             return self[0, 0] * self[1, 1] - self[0, 1] * self[1, 0]
1985         elif n == 3:
1986             return  (self[0, 0] * self[1, 1] * self[2, 2]
1987                    + self[0, 1] * self[1, 2] * self[2, 0]
1988                    + self[0, 2] * self[1, 0] * self[2, 1]
1989                    - self[0, 2] * self[1, 1] * self[2, 0]
1990                    - self[0, 0] * self[1, 2] * self[2, 1]
1991                    - self[0, 1] * self[1, 0] * self[2, 2])
1992 
1993         if method == "bareiss":
1994             return self._eval_det_bareiss()
1995         elif method == "berkowitz":
1996             return self._eval_det_berkowitz()
1997         elif method == "lu":
1998             return self._eval_det_lu()

2088     def _matrix_pow_by_jordan_blocks(self, num):
2089         from sympy.matrices import diag, MutableMatrix
2090         from sympy import binomial
2091 
2092         def jordan_cell_power(jc, n):
2093             N = jc.shape[0]
2094             l = jc[0, 0]
2095             if l == 0 and (n < N - 1) != False:
2096                 raise ValueError("Matrix det == 0; not invertible")
2097             elif l == 0 and N > 1 and n % 1 != 0:
2098                 raise ValueError("Non-integer power cannot be evaluated")
2099             for i in range(N):
2100                 for j in range(N-i):
2101                     bn = binomial(n, i)
2102                     if isinstance(bn, binomial):
2103                         bn = bn._eval_expand_func()
2104                     jc[j, i+j] = l**(n-i)*bn
2105 
2106         P, jordan_cells = self.jordan_cells()
2107         # Make sure jordan_cells matrices are mutable:
2108         jordan_cells = [MutableMatrix(j) for j in jordan_cells]
2109         for j in jordan_cells:
2110             jordan_cell_power(j, num)
2111         return self._new(P*diag(*jordan_cells)*P.inv())

2113     def _matrix_pow_by_recursion(self, num):
2114         from sympy.matrices import eye
2115         n = int(num)

2117             return self.inv()**-n   # A**-2 = (A**-1)**2
2118         a = eye(self.cols)
2119         s = self
2120         while n:
2121             if n % 2:
2122                 a *= s
2123                 n -= 1
2124             if not n:
2125                 break
2126             s *= s
2127             n //= 2
2128         return self._new(a)

2298     def _jordan_block_structure(self):
2299         # To every eigenvalue may belong `i` blocks with size s(i)
2300         # and a chain of generalized eigenvectors
2301         # which will be determined by the following computations:
2302         # for every eigenvalue we will add a dictionary
2303         # containing, for all blocks, the blocksizes and the attached chain vectors
2304         # that will eventually be used to form the transformation P
2305         jordan_block_structures = {}
2306         _eigenvects = self.eigenvects()
2307         ev = self.eigenvals()
2308         if len(ev) == 0:
2309             raise AttributeError("could not compute the eigenvalues")
2310         for eigenval, multiplicity, vects in _eigenvects:
2311             l_jordan_chains = {}
2312             geometrical = len(vects)
2313             if geometrical == multiplicity:
2314                 # The Jordan chains have all length 1 and consist of only one vector
2315                 # which is the eigenvector of course
2316                 chains = []
2317                 for v in vects:
2318                     chain = [v]
2319                     chains.append(chain)
2320                 l_jordan_chains[1] = chains
2321                 jordan_block_structures[eigenval] = l_jordan_chains
2322             elif geometrical == 0:
2323                 raise MatrixError(
2324                     "Matrix has the eigen vector with geometrical multiplicity equal zero.")
2325             else:
2326                 # Up to now we know nothing about the sizes of the blocks of our Jordan matrix.
2327                 # Note that knowledge of algebraic and geometrical multiplicity
2328                 # will *NOT* be sufficient to determine this structure.
2329                 # The blocksize `s` could be defined as the minimal `k` where
2330                 # `kernel(self-lI)^k = kernel(self-lI)^(k+1)`
2331                 # The extreme case would be that k = (multiplicity-geometrical+1)
2332                 # but the blocks could be smaller.
2333 
2334                 # Consider for instance the following matrix
2335 
2336                 # [2 1 0 0]
2337                 # [0 2 1 0]
2338                 # [0 0 2 0]
2339                 # [0 0 0 2]
2340 
2341                 # which coincides with it own Jordan canonical form.
2342                 # It has only one eigenvalue l=2 of (algebraic) multiplicity=4.
2343                 # It has two eigenvectors, one belonging to the last row (blocksize 1)
2344                 # and one being the last part of a jordan chain of length 3 (blocksize of the first block).
2345 
2346                 # Note again that it is not not possible to obtain this from the algebraic and geometrical
2347                 # multiplicity alone. This only gives us an upper limit for the dimension of one of
2348                 # the subspaces (blocksize of according jordan block) given by
2349                 # max=(multiplicity-geometrical+1) which is reached for our matrix
2350                 # but not for
2351 
2352                 # [2 1 0 0]
2353                 # [0 2 0 0]
2354                 # [0 0 2 1]
2355                 # [0 0 0 2]
2356 
2357                 # although multiplicity=4 and geometrical=2 are the same for this matrix.
2358 
2359                 from sympy.matrices import MutableMatrix
2360                 I = MutableMatrix.eye(self.rows)
2361                 l = eigenval
2362                 M = (self - l * I)
2363 
2364                 # We will store the matrices `(self-l*I)^k` for further computations
2365                 # for convenience only we store `Ms[0]=(sefl-lI)^0=I`
2366                 # so the index is the same as the power for all further Ms entries
2367                 # We also store the vectors that span these kernels (Ns[0] = [])
2368                 # and also their dimensions `a_s`
2369                 # this is mainly done for debugging since the number of blocks of a given size
2370                 # can be computed from the a_s, in order to check our result which is obtained simpler
2371                 # by counting the number of Jordan chains for `a` given `s`
2372                 # `a_0` is `dim(Kernel(Ms[0]) = dim (Kernel(I)) = 0` since `I` is regular
2373 
2374                 l_jordan_chains = {}
2375                 Ms = [I]
2376                 Ns = [[]]
2377                 a = [0]
2378                 smax = 0
2379                 M_new = Ms[-1] * M
2380                 Ns_new = M_new.nullspace()
2381                 a_new = len(Ns_new)
2382                 Ms.append(M_new)
2383                 Ns.append(Ns_new)
2384                 while a_new > a[
2385                     -1]:  # as long as the nullspaces increase compute further powers
2386                     a.append(a_new)
2387                     M_new = Ms[-1] * M
2388                     Ns_new = M_new.nullspace()
2389                     a_new = len(Ns_new)
2390                     Ms.append(M_new)
2391                     Ns.append(Ns_new)
2392                     smax += 1
2393 
2394                 # We now have `Ms[-1]=((self-l*I)**s)=Z=0`.
2395                 # We also know the size of the biggest Jordan block
2396                 # associated with `l` to be `s`.
2397                 # Now let us proceed with the computation of the associate part of the transformation matrix `P`.
2398                 # We already know the kernel (=nullspace)  `K_l` of (self-lI) which consists of the
2399                 # eigenvectors belonging to eigenvalue `l`.
2400                 # The dimension of this space is the geometric multiplicity of eigenvalue `l`.
2401                 # For every eigenvector ev out of `K_l`, there exists a subspace that is
2402                 # spanned by the Jordan chain of ev. The dimension of this subspace is
2403                 # represented by the length `s` of the Jordan block.
2404                 # The chain itself is given by `{e_0,..,e_s-1}` where:
2405                 # `e_k+1 =(self-lI)e_k (*)`
2406                 # and
2407                 # `e_s-1=ev`
2408                 # So it would be possible to start with the already known `ev` and work backwards until one
2409                 # reaches `e_0`. Unfortunately this can not be done by simply solving system (*) since its matrix
2410                 # is singular (by definition of the eigenspaces).
2411                 # This approach would force us a choose in every step the degree of freedom undetermined
2412                 # by (*). This is difficult to implement with computer algebra systems and also quite inefficient.
2413                 # We therefore reformulate the problem in terms of nullspaces.
2414                 # To do so we start from the other end and choose `e0`'s out of
2415                 # `E=Kernel(self-lI)^s / Kernel(self-lI)^(s-1)`
2416                 # Note that `Kernel(self-lI)^s = Kernel(Z) = V` (the whole vector space).
2417                 # So in the first step `s=smax` this restriction turns out to actually restrict nothing at all
2418                 # and the only remaining condition is to choose vectors in `Kernel(self-lI)^(s-1)`.
2419                 # Subsequently we compute `e_1=(self-lI)e_0`, `e_2=(self-lI)*e_1` and so on.
2420                 # The subspace `E` can have a dimension larger than one.
2421                 # That means that we have more than one Jordan block of size `s` for the eigenvalue `l`
2422                 # and as many Jordan chains (this is the case in the second example).
2423                 # In this case we start as many Jordan chains and have as many blocks of size `s` in the jcf.
2424                 # We now have all the Jordan blocks of size `s` but there might be others attached to the same
2425                 # eigenvalue that are smaller.
2426                 # So we will do the same procedure also for `s-1` and so on until 1 (the lowest possible order
2427                 # where the Jordan chain is of length 1 and just represented by the eigenvector).
2428 
2429                 for s in reversed(range(1, smax + 1)):
2430                     S = Ms[s]
2431                     # We want the vectors in `Kernel((self-lI)^s)`,
2432                     # but without those in `Kernel(self-lI)^s-1`
2433                     # so we will add their adjoints as additional equations
2434                     # to the system formed by `S` to get the orthogonal
2435                     # complement.
2436                     # (`S` will no longer be quadratic.)
2437 
2438                     exclude_vectors = Ns[s - 1]
2439                     for k in range(0, a[s - 1]):
2440                         S = S.col_join((exclude_vectors[k]).adjoint())
2441 
2442                     # We also want to exclude the vectors
2443                     # in the chains for the bigger blocks
2444                     # that we have already computed (if there are any).
2445                     # (That is why we start with the biggest s).
2446 
2447                     # Since Jordan blocks are not orthogonal in general
2448                     # (in the original space), only those chain vectors
2449                     # that are on level s (index `s-1` in a chain)
2450                     # are added.
2451 
2452                     for chain_list in l_jordan_chains.values():
2453                         for chain in chain_list:
2454                             S = S.col_join(chain[s - 1].adjoint())
2455 
2456                     e0s = S.nullspace()
2457                     # Determine the number of chain leaders
2458                     # for blocks of size `s`.
2459                     n_e0 = len(e0s)
2460                     s_chains = []
2461                     # s_cells=[]
2462                     for i in range(0, n_e0):
2463                         chain = [e0s[i]]
2464                         for k in range(1, s):
2465                             v = M * chain[k - 1]
2466                             chain.append(v)
2467 
2468                         # We want the chain leader appear as the last of the block.
2469                         chain.reverse()
2470                         s_chains.append(chain)
2471                     l_jordan_chains[s] = s_chains
2472             jordan_block_structures[eigenval] = l_jordan_chains
2473         return jordan_block_structures
2474 
2475     def _jordan_split(self, algebraical, geometrical):
2476         """Return a list of integers with sum equal to 'algebraical'
2477         and length equal to 'geometrical'"""
2478         n1 = algebraical // geometrical
2479         res = [n1] * geometrical
2480         res[len(res) - 1] += algebraical % geometrical
2481         assert sum(res) == algebraical

2639     def berkowitz(self):
2640         """The Berkowitz algorithm.
2641 
2642            Given N x N matrix with symbolic content, compute efficiently
2643            coefficients of characteristic polynomials of 'self' and all
2644            its square sub-matrices composed by removing both i-th row
2645            and column, without division in the ground domain.
2646 
2647            This method is particularly useful for computing determinant,
2648            principal minors and characteristic polynomial, when 'self'
2649            has complicated coefficients e.g. polynomials. Semi-direct
2650            usage of this algorithm is also important in computing
2651            efficiently sub-resultant PRS.
2652 
2653            Assuming that M is a square matrix of dimension N x N and
2654            I is N x N identity matrix,  then the following following
2655            definition of characteristic polynomial is begin used:
2656 
2657                           charpoly(M) = det(t*I - M)
2658 
2659            As a consequence, all polynomials generated by Berkowitz
2660            algorithm are monic.
2661 
2662            >>> from sympy import Matrix
2663            >>> from sympy.abc import x, y, z
2664 
2665            >>> M = Matrix([[x, y, z], [1, 0, 0], [y, z, x]])
2666 
2667            >>> p, q, r, s = M.berkowitz()
2668 
2669            >>> p # 0 x 0 M's sub-matrix
2670            (1,)
2671 
2672            >>> q # 1 x 1 M's sub-matrix
2673            (1, -x)
2674 
2675            >>> r # 2 x 2 M's sub-matrix
2676            (1, -x, -y)
2677 
2678            >>> s # 3 x 3 M's sub-matrix
2679            (1, -2*x, x**2 - y*z - y, x*y - z**2)
2680 
2681            For more information on the implemented algorithm refer to:
2682 
2683            [1] S.J. Berkowitz, On computing the determinant in small
2684                parallel time using a small number of processors, ACM,
2685                Information Processing Letters 18, 1984, pp. 147-150
2686 
2687            [2] M. Keber, Division-Free computation of sub-resultants
2688                using Bezout matrices, Tech. Report MPI-I-2006-1-006,
2689                Saarbrucken, 2006
2690 
2691         See Also
2692         ========
2693 
2694         berkowitz_det
2695         berkowitz_minors
2696         berkowitz_charpoly
2697         berkowitz_eigenvals
2698         """
2699         from sympy.matrices import zeros
2700         berk = ((1,),)
2701         if not self:
2702             return berk
2703 
2704         if not self.is_square:
2705             raise NonSquareMatrixError()
2706 
2707         A, N = self, self.rows
2708         transforms = [0] * (N - 1)
2709 
2710         for n in range(N, 1, -1):
2711             T, k = zeros(n + 1, n), n - 1
2712 
2713             R, C = -A[k, :k], A[:k, k]
2714             A, a = A[:k, :k], -A[k, k]
2715 
2716             items = [C]
2717 
2718             for i in range(0, n - 2):
2719                 items.append(A * items[i])
2720 
2721             for i, B in enumerate(items):
2722                 items[i] = (R * B)[0, 0]
2723 
2724             items = [S.One, a] + items
2725 
2726             for i in range(n):
2727                 T[i:, i] = items[:n - i + 1]
2728 
2729             transforms[k - 1] = T
2730 
2731         polys = [self._new([S.One, -A[0, 0]])]
2732 
2733         for i, T in enumerate(transforms):
2734             polys.append(T * polys[i])
2735 
2736         return berk + tuple(map(tuple, polys))
2737 
2738     def cholesky_solve(self, rhs):
2739         """Solves Ax = B using Cholesky decomposition,
2740         for a general square non-singular matrix.
2741         For a non-square matrix with rows > cols,
2742         the least squares solution is returned.
2743 
2744         See Also
2745         ========
2746 
2747         lower_triangular_solve
2748         upper_triangular_solve
2749         gauss_jordan_solve
2750         diagonal_solve
2751         LDLsolve
2752         LUsolve
2753         QRsolve
2754         pinv_solve
2755         """
2756         if self.is_symmetric():
2757             L = self._cholesky()
2758         elif self.rows >= self.cols:
2759             L = (self.T * self)._cholesky()
2760             rhs = self.T * rhs
2761         else:
2762             raise NotImplementedError('Under-determined System. '
2763                                       'Try M.gauss_jordan_solve(rhs)')
2764         Y = L._lower_triangular_solve(rhs)
2765         return (L.T)._upper_triangular_solve(Y)

2767     def cholesky(self):
2768         """Returns the Cholesky decomposition L of a matrix A
2769         such that L * L.T = A

2885     def cross(self, b):
2886         """Return the cross product of `self` and `b` relaxing the condition
2887         of compatible dimensions: if each has 3 elements, a matrix of the
2888         same type and shape as `self` will be returned. If `b` has the same
2889         shape as `self` then common identities for the cross product (like
2890         `a x b = - b x a`) will hold.

2893         ========
2894

2896         multiply
2897         multiply_elementwise

2899         if not is_sequence(b):
2900             raise TypeError(
2901                 "`b` must be an ordered iterable or Matrix, not %s." %
2902                 type(b))

2904             raise ShapeError("Dimensions incorrect for cross product: %s x %s" %
2905                              ((self.rows, self.cols), (b.rows, b.cols)))
2906         else:
2907             return self._new(self.rows, self.cols, (
2908                 (self[1] * b[2] - self[2] * b[1]),
2909                 (self[2] * b[0] - self[0] * b[2]),
2910                 (self[0] * b[1] - self[1] * b[0])))

2959     def det_bareiss(self):
2960         """Compute matrix determinant using Bareiss' fraction-free
2961         algorithm which is an extension of the well known Gaussian
2962         elimination method. This approach is best suited for dense
2963         symbolic matrices and will result in a determinant with
2964         minimal number of fractions. It means that less term
2965         rewriting is needed on resulting formulae.
2966 
2967         TODO: Implement algorithm for sparse matrices (SFF),
2968         http://www.eecis.udel.edu/~saunders/papers/sffge/it5.ps.
2969 
2970         See Also
2971         ========
2972 
2973         det
2974         berkowitz_det
2975         """
2976         if not self.is_square:
2977             raise NonSquareMatrixError()
2978         if not self:
2979             return S.One
2980 
2981         M, n = self.copy().as_mutable(), self.rows
2982 
2983         if n == 1:
2984             det = M[0, 0]
2985         elif n == 2:
2986             det = M[0, 0] * M[1, 1] - M[0, 1] * M[1, 0]
2987         elif n == 3:
2988             det = (
2989                   M[0, 0] * M[1, 1] * M[2, 2] + M[0, 1] * M[1, 2] * M[2, 0] + M[
2990                       0, 2] * M[1, 0] * M[2, 1]) - \
2991                   (
2992                   M[0, 2] * M[1, 1] * M[2, 0] + M[0, 0] * M[1, 2] * M[2, 1] + M[
2993                       0, 1] * M[1, 0] * M[2, 2])
2994         else:
2995             sign = 1  # track current sign in case of column swap
2996 
2997             for k in range(n - 1):
2998                 # look for a pivot in the current column
2999                 # and assume det == 0 if none is found
3000                 if M[k, k] == 0:
3001                     for i in range(k + 1, n):
3002                         if M[i, k]:
3003                             M.row_swap(i, k)
3004                             sign *= -1
3005                             break
3006                     else:
3007                         return S.Zero
3008 
3009                 # proceed with Bareiss' fraction-free (FF)
3010                 # form of Gaussian elimination algorithm
3011                 for i in range(k + 1, n):
3012                     for j in range(k + 1, n):
3013                         D = M[k, k] * M[i, j] - M[i, k] * M[k, j]
3014 
3015                         if k > 0:
3016                             D /= M[k - 1, k - 1]
3017 
3018                         if D.is_Atom:
3019                             M[i, j] = D
3020                         else:
3021                             M[i, j] = cancel(D)
3022 
3023             det = sign * M[n - 1, n - 1]
3024 
3025         return det.expand()
3026 
3027     def det_LU_decomposition(self):
3028         """Compute matrix determinant using LU decomposition
3029 
3030 
3031         Note that this method fails if the LU decomposition itself
3032         fails. In particular, if the matrix has no inverse this method
3033         will fail.
3034 
3035         TODO: Implement algorithm for sparse matrices (SFF),
3036         http://www.eecis.udel.edu/~saunders/papers/sffge/it5.ps.
3037 
3038         See Also
3039         ========
3040 
3041 
3042         det
3043         det_bareiss
3044         berkowitz_det
3045         """
3046         if not self.is_square:
3047             raise NonSquareMatrixError()
3048         if not self:
3049             return S.One
3050 
3051         M, n = self.copy(), self.rows
3052         p, prod = [], 1
3053         l, u, p = M.LUdecomposition()
3054         if len(p) % 2:
3055             prod = -1
3056 
3057         for k in range(n):
3058             prod = prod * u[k, k] * l[k, k]
3059 
3060         return prod.expand()

3093     def diagonalize(self, reals_only=False, sort=False, normalize=False):
3094         """
3095         Return (P, D), where D is diagonal and
3096 
3097             D = P^-1 * M * P
3098 
3099         where M is current matrix.
3100 
3101         Examples
3102         ========
3103 
3104         >>> from sympy import Matrix
3105         >>> m = Matrix(3, 3, [1, 2, 0, 0, 3, 0, 2, -4, 2])
3106         >>> m
3107         Matrix([
3108         [1,  2, 0],
3109         [0,  3, 0],
3110         [2, -4, 2]])
3111         >>> (P, D) = m.diagonalize()
3112         >>> D
3113         Matrix([
3114         [1, 0, 0],
3115         [0, 2, 0],
3116         [0, 0, 3]])
3117         >>> P
3118         Matrix([
3119         [-1, 0, -1],
3120         [ 0, 0, -1],
3121         [ 2, 1,  2]])
3122         >>> P.inv() * m * P
3123         Matrix([
3124         [1, 0, 0],
3125         [0, 2, 0],
3126         [0, 0, 3]])
3127 
3128         See Also
3129         ========
3130 
3131         is_diagonal
3132         is_diagonalizable
3133 
3134         """
3135         from sympy.matrices import diag
3136 
3137         if not self.is_square:
3138             raise NonSquareMatrixError()
3139         if not self.is_diagonalizable(reals_only, False):
3140             self._diagonalize_clear_subproducts()
3141             raise MatrixError("Matrix is not diagonalizable")
3142         else:
3143             if self._eigenvects is None:
3144                 self._eigenvects = self.eigenvects(simplify=True)
3145             if sort:
3146                 self._eigenvects.sort(key=default_sort_key)
3147                 self._eigenvects.reverse()
3148             diagvals = []
3149             P = self._new(self.rows, 0, [])
3150             for eigenval, multiplicity, vects in self._eigenvects:
3151                 for k in range(multiplicity):
3152                     diagvals.append(eigenval)
3153                     vec = vects[k]
3154                     if normalize:
3155                         vec = vec / vec.norm()
3156                     P = P.col_insert(P.cols, vec)
3157             D = diag(*diagvals)
3158             self._diagonalize_clear_subproducts()
3159             return (P, D)

3184     def dot(self, b):
3185         """Return the dot product of Matrix self and b relaxing the condition
3186         of compatible dimensions: if either the number of rows or columns are
3187         the same as the length of b then the dot product is returned. If self
3188         is a row or column vector, a scalar is returned. Otherwise, a list
3189         of results is returned (and in that case the number of columns in self
3190         must match the length of b).
3191 
3192         Examples
3193         ========
3194 
3195         >>> from sympy import Matrix
3196         >>> M = Matrix([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 9]])
3197         >>> v = [1, 1, 1]
3198         >>> M.row(0).dot(v)
3199         6
3200         >>> M.col(0).dot(v)
3201         12
3202         >>> M.dot(v)
3203         [6, 15, 24]
3204 
3205         See Also
3206         ========
3207 
3208         cross
3209         multiply
3210         multiply_elementwise
3211         """
3212         from .dense import Matrix
3213 
3214         if not isinstance(b, MatrixBase):
3215             if is_sequence(b):
3216                 if len(b) != self.cols and len(b) != self.rows:
3217                     raise ShapeError(
3218                         "Dimensions incorrect for dot product: %s, %s" % (
3219                             self.shape, len(b)))
3220                 return self.dot(Matrix(b))
3221             else:
3222                 raise TypeError(
3223                     "`b` must be an ordered iterable or Matrix, not %s." %
3224                     type(b))
3225 
3226         mat = self
3227         if mat.cols == b.rows:
3228             if b.cols != 1:
3229                 mat = mat.T
3230                 b = b.T
3231             prod = flatten((mat * b).tolist())
3232             if len(prod) == 1:
3233                 return prod[0]
3234             return prod
3235         if mat.cols == b.cols:
3236             return mat.dot(b.T)
3237         elif mat.rows == b.rows:
3238             return mat.T.dot(b)
3239         else:
3240             raise ShapeError("Dimensions incorrect for dot product: %s, %s" % (
3241                 self.shape, b.shape))

3243     def dual(self):
3244         """Returns the dual of a matrix, which is:
3245 
3246         `(1/2)*levicivita(i, j, k, l)*M(k, l)` summed over indices `k` and `l`
3247 
3248         Since the levicivita method is anti_symmetric for any pairwise
3249         exchange of indices, the dual of a symmetric matrix is the zero
3250         matrix. Strictly speaking the dual defined here assumes that the
3251         'matrix' `M` is a contravariant anti_symmetric second rank tensor,
3252         so that the dual is a covariant second rank tensor.
3253 
3254         """
3255         from sympy import LeviCivita
3256         from sympy.matrices import zeros
3257 
3258         M, n = self[:, :], self.rows
3259         work = zeros(n)
3260         if self.is_symmetric():
3261             return work
3262 
3263         for i in range(1, n):
3264             for j in range(1, n):
3265                 acum = 0
3266                 for k in range(1, n):
3267                     acum += LeviCivita(i, j, 0, k) * M[0, k]
3268                 work[i, j] = acum
3269                 work[j, i] = -acum
3270 
3271         for l in range(1, n):
3272             acum = 0
3273             for a in range(1, n):
3274                 for b in range(1, n):
3275                     acum += LeviCivita(0, l, a, b) * M[a, b]
3276             acum /= 2
3277             work[0, l] = -acum
3278             work[l, 0] = acum
3279 
3280         return work

3282     def eigenvals(self, **flags):
3283         """Return eigen values using the berkowitz_eigenvals routine.
3284 
3285         Since the roots routine doesn't always work well with Floats,
3286         they will be replaced with Rationals before calling that
3287         routine. If this is not desired, set flag ``rational`` to False.
3288         """
3289         # roots doesn't like Floats, so replace them with Rationals
3290         # unless the nsimplify flag indicates that this has already
3291         # been done, e.g. in eigenvects
3292         mat = self
3293 
3294         if not mat:
3295             return {}
3296         if flags.pop('rational', True):
3297             if any(v.has(Float) for v in mat):
3298                 mat = mat._new(mat.rows, mat.cols,
3299                                [nsimplify(v, rational=True) for v in mat])
3300

3302         return mat.berkowitz_eigenvals(**flags)

3304     def eigenvects(self, **flags):
3305         """Return list of triples (eigenval, multiplicity, basis).
3306 
3307         The flag ``simplify`` has two effects:
3308             1) if bool(simplify) is True, as_content_primitive()
3309             will be used to tidy up normalization artifacts;
3310             2) if nullspace needs simplification to compute the
3311             basis, the simplify flag will be passed on to the
3312             nullspace routine which will interpret it there.
3313 
3314         If the matrix contains any Floats, they will be changed to Rationals
3315         for computation purposes, but the answers will be returned after being
3316         evaluated with evalf. If it is desired to removed small imaginary
3317         portions during the evalf step, pass a value for the ``chop`` flag.
3318         """
3319         from sympy.matrices import eye
3320 
3321         simplify = flags.get('simplify', True)
3322         primitive = bool(flags.get('simplify', False))
3323         chop = flags.pop('chop', False)
3324 
3325         flags.pop('multiple', None)  # remove this if it's there
3326 
3327         # roots doesn't like Floats, so replace them with Rationals
3328         float = False
3329         mat = self
3330         if any(v.has(Float) for v in self):
3331             float = True
3332             mat = mat._new(mat.rows, mat.cols, [nsimplify(
3333                 v, rational=True) for v in mat])
3334             flags['rational'] = False  # to tell eigenvals not to do this
3335 
3336         out, vlist = [], mat.eigenvals(**flags)
3337         vlist = list(vlist.items())
3338         vlist.sort(key=default_sort_key)
3339         flags.pop('rational', None)
3340 
3341         for r, k in vlist:
3342             tmp = mat.as_mutable() - eye(mat.rows) * r
3343             basis = tmp.nullspace()
3344             # whether tmp.is_symbolic() is True or False, it is possible that
3345             # the basis will come back as [] in which case simplification is
3346             # necessary.
3347             if not basis:
3348                 # The nullspace routine failed, try it again with simplification
3349                 basis = tmp.nullspace(simplify=simplify)
3350                 if not basis:
3351                     raise NotImplementedError(
3352                         "Can't evaluate eigenvector for eigenvalue %s" % r)
3353             if primitive:
3354                 # the relationship A*e = lambda*e will still hold if we change the
3355                 # eigenvector; so if simplify is True we tidy up any normalization
3356                 # artifacts with as_content_primtive (default) and remove any pure Integer
3357                 # denominators.
3358                 l = 1
3359                 for i, b in enumerate(basis[0]):
3360                     c, p = signsimp(b).as_content_primitive()
3361                     if c is not S.One:
3362                         b = c * p
3363                         l = ilcm(l, c.q)
3364                     basis[0][i] = b
3365                 if l != 1:
3366                     basis[0] *= l
3367             if float:
3368                 out.append((r.evalf(chop=chop), k, [
3369                     mat._new(b).evalf(chop=chop) for b in basis]))
3370             else:
3371                 out.append((r, k, [mat._new(b) for b in basis]))
3372         return out

3374     def exp(self):
3375         """Return the exponentiation of a square matrix."""
3376         if not self.is_square:
3377             raise NonSquareMatrixError(
3378                 "Exponentiation is valid only for square matrices")
3379         try:
3380             P, cells = self.jordan_cells()
3381         except MatrixError:
3382             raise NotImplementedError(
3383                 "Exponentiation is implemented only for matrices for which the Jordan normal form can be computed")
3384 
3385         def _jblock_exponential(b):
3386             # This function computes the matrix exponential for one single Jordan block
3387             nr = b.rows
3388             l = b[0, 0]
3389             if nr == 1:
3390                 res = exp(l)
3391             else:
3392                 from sympy import eye
3393                 # extract the diagonal part
3394                 d = b[0, 0] * eye(nr)
3395                 # and the nilpotent part
3396                 n = b - d
3397                 # compute its exponential
3398                 nex = eye(nr)
3399                 for i in range(1, nr):
3400                     nex = nex + n ** i / factorial(i)
3401                 # combine the two parts
3402                 res = exp(b[0, 0]) * nex
3403             return (res)
3404 
3405         blocks = list(map(_jblock_exponential, cells))
3406         from sympy.matrices import diag
3407         eJ = diag(*blocks)
3408         # n = self.rows
3409         ret = P * eJ * P.inv()
3410         return type(self)(ret)

3412     def gauss_jordan_solve(self, b, freevar=False):
3413         """
3414         Solves Ax = b using Gauss Jordan elimination.
3415 
3416         There may be zero, one, or infinite solutions.  If one solution
3417         exists, it will be returned. If infinite solutions exist, it will
3418         be returned parametrically. If no solutions exist, It will throw
3419         ValueError.
3420 
3421         Parameters
3422         ==========
3423 
3424         b : Matrix
3425             The right hand side of the equation to be solved for.  Must have
3426             the same number of rows as matrix A.
3427 
3428         freevar : List
3429             If the system is underdetermined (e.g. A has more columns than
3430             rows), infinite solutions are possible, in terms of an arbitrary
3431             values of free variables. Then the index of the free variables
3432             in the solutions (column Matrix) will be returned by freevar, if
3433             the flag `freevar` is set to `True`.
3434 
3435         Returns
3436         =======
3437 
3438         x : Matrix
3439             The matrix that will satisfy Ax = B.  Will have as many rows as
3440             matrix A has columns, and as many columns as matrix B.
3441 
3442         params : Matrix
3443             If the system is underdetermined (e.g. A has more columns than
3444             rows), infinite solutions are possible, in terms of an arbitrary
3445             parameters. These arbitrary parameters are returned as params
3446             Matrix.
3447 
3448         Examples
3449         ========
3450 
3451         >>> from sympy import Matrix
3452         >>> A = Matrix([[1, 2, 1, 1], [1, 2, 2, -1], [2, 4, 0, 6]])
3453         >>> b = Matrix([7, 12, 4])
3454         >>> sol, params = A.gauss_jordan_solve(b)
3455         >>> sol
3456         Matrix([
3457         [-2*_tau0 - 3*_tau1 + 2],
3458         [                 _tau0],
3459         [           2*_tau1 + 5],
3460         [                 _tau1]])
3461         >>> params
3462         Matrix([
3463         [_tau0],
3464         [_tau1]])
3465 
3466         >>> A = Matrix([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 10]])
3467         >>> b = Matrix([3, 6, 9])
3468         >>> sol, params = A.gauss_jordan_solve(b)
3469         >>> sol
3470         Matrix([
3471         [-1],
3472         [ 2],
3473         [ 0]])
3474         >>> params
3475         Matrix(0, 1, [])
3476 
3477         See Also
3478         ========
3479 
3480         lower_triangular_solve
3481         upper_triangular_solve
3482         cholesky_solve
3483         diagonal_solve
3484         LDLsolve
3485         LUsolve
3486         QRsolve
3487         pinv
3488 
3489         References
3490         ==========
3491 
3492         .. [1] http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_elimination
3493 
3494         """
3495         from sympy.matrices import Matrix, zeros
3496 
3497         aug = self.hstack(self.copy(), b.copy())
3498         row, col = aug[:, :-1].shape
3499 
3500         # solve by reduced row echelon form
3501         A, pivots = aug.rref(simplify=True)
3502         A, v = A[:, :-1], A[:, -1]
3503         pivots = list(filter(lambda p: p < col, pivots))
3504         rank = len(pivots)
3505 
3506         # Bring to block form
3507         permutation = Matrix(range(col)).T
3508         A = A.vstack(A, permutation)
3509 
3510         for i, c in enumerate(pivots):
3511             A.col_swap(i, c)
3512 
3513         A, permutation = A[:-1, :], A[-1, :]
3514 
3515         # check for existence of solutions
3516         # rank of aug Matrix should be equal to rank of coefficient matrix
3517         if not v[rank:, 0].is_zero:
3518             raise ValueError("Linear system has no solution")
3519 
3520         # Get index of free symbols (free parameters)
3521         free_var_index = permutation[
3522                          len(pivots):]  # non-pivots columns are free variables
3523 
3524         # Free parameters
3525         dummygen = numbered_symbols("tau", Dummy)
3526         tau = Matrix([next(dummygen) for k in range(col - rank)]).reshape(
3527             col - rank, 1)
3528 
3529         # Full parametric solution
3530         V = A[:rank, rank:]
3531         vt = v[:rank, 0]
3532         free_sol = tau.vstack(vt - V * tau, tau)
3533 
3534         # Undo permutation
3535         sol = zeros(col, 1)
3536         for k, v in enumerate(free_sol):
3537             sol[permutation[k], 0] = v
3538 
3539         if freevar:
3540             return sol, tau, free_var_index
3541         else:
3542             return sol, tau

3588     def inv_mod(self, m):
3589         """
3590         Returns the inverse of the matrix `K` (mod `m`), if it exists.
3591 
3592         Method to find the matrix inverse of `K` (mod `m`) implemented in this function:
3593 
3594         * Compute `\mathrm{adj}(K) = \mathrm{cof}(K)^t`, the adjoint matrix of `K`.
3595 
3596         * Compute `r = 1/\mathrm{det}(K) \pmod m`.
3597 
3598         * `K^{-1} = r\cdot \mathrm{adj}(K) \pmod m`.
3599 
3600         Examples
3601         ========
3602 
3603         >>> from sympy import Matrix
3604         >>> A = Matrix(2, 2, [1, 2, 3, 4])
3605         >>> A.inv_mod(5)
3606         Matrix([
3607         [3, 1],
3608         [4, 2]])
3609         >>> A.inv_mod(3)
3610         Matrix([
3611         [1, 1],
3612         [0, 1]])
3613 
3614         """
3615         from sympy.ntheory import totient
3616         if not self.is_square:
3617             raise NonSquareMatrixError()
3618         N = self.cols
3619         phi = totient(m)
3620         det_K = self.det()
3621         if gcd(det_K, m) != 1:
3622             raise ValueError('Matrix is not invertible (mod %d)' % m)
3623         det_inv = pow(int(det_K), int(phi - 1), int(m))
3624         K_adj = self.cofactorMatrix().transpose()
3625         K_inv = self.__class__(N, N,
3626                                [det_inv * K_adj[i, j] % m for i in range(N) for
3627                                 j in range(N)])
3628         return K_inv
3629 
3630     def inverse_ADJ(self, iszerofunc=_iszero):
3631         """Calculates the inverse using the adjugate matrix and a determinant.
3632 
3633         See Also
3634         ========
3635 
3636         inv
3637         inverse_LU
3638         inverse_GE
3639         """
3640         if not self.is_square:
3641             raise NonSquareMatrixError("A Matrix must be square to invert.")
3642 
3643         d = self.berkowitz_det()
3644         zero = d.equals(0)
3645         if zero is None:
3646             # if equals() can't decide, will rref be able to?
3647             ok = self.rref(simplify=True)[0]
3648             zero = any(iszerofunc(ok[j, j]) for j in range(ok.rows))
3649         if zero:
3650             raise ValueError("Matrix det == 0; not invertible.")
3651 
3652         return self.adjugate() / d

3654     def inverse_GE(self, iszerofunc=_iszero):

3661         inverse_LU

3669         red = big.rref(iszerofunc=iszerofunc, simplify=True)[0]
3670         if any(iszerofunc(red[j, j]) for j in range(red.rows)):
3671             raise ValueError("Matrix det == 0; not invertible.")
3672 
3673         return self._new(red[:, big.rows:])

3786         >>> m
3787         Matrix([
3788         [ 0, 1],
3789         [-1, 0]])
3790         >>> m.is_diagonalizable()
3791         True
3792         >>> m.is_diagonalizable(True)
3793         False
3794 
3795         See Also
3796         ========
3797 
3798         is_diagonal
3799         diagonalize
3800         """
3801         if not self.is_square:
3802             return False
3803         res = False
3804         self._is_symbolic = self.is_symbolic()
3805         self._is_symmetric = self.is_symmetric()
3806         self._eigenvects = None
3807         self._eigenvects = self.eigenvects(simplify=True)
3808         all_iscorrect = True
3809         for eigenval, multiplicity, vects in self._eigenvects:
3810             if len(vects) != multiplicity:
3811                 all_iscorrect = False
3812                 break
3813             elif reals_only and not eigenval.is_real:
3814                 all_iscorrect = False
3815                 break
3816         res = all_iscorrect
3817         if clear_subproducts:
3818             self._diagonalize_clear_subproducts()

3821     def is_nilpotent(self):

3825         a zero matrix.

3849     def jacobian(self, X):
3850         """Calculates the Jacobian matrix (derivative of a vectorial function).
3851 
3852         Parameters
3853         ==========
3854 
3855         self : vector of expressions representing functions f_i(x_1, ..., x_n).
3856         X : set of x_i's in order, it can be a list or a Matrix
3857 
3858         Both self and X can be a row or a column matrix in any order
3859         (i.e., jacobian() should always work).
3860 
3861         Examples
3862         ========
3863 
3864         >>> from sympy import sin, cos, Matrix
3865         >>> from sympy.abc import rho, phi
3866         >>> X = Matrix([rho*cos(phi), rho*sin(phi), rho**2])
3867         >>> Y = Matrix([rho, phi])
3868         >>> X.jacobian(Y)
3869         Matrix([
3870         [cos(phi), -rho*sin(phi)],
3871         [sin(phi),  rho*cos(phi)],
3872         [   2*rho,             0]])
3873         >>> X = Matrix([rho*cos(phi), rho*sin(phi)])
3874         >>> X.jacobian(Y)
3875         Matrix([
3876         [cos(phi), -rho*sin(phi)],
3877         [sin(phi),  rho*cos(phi)]])
3878 
3879         See Also
3880         ========
3881 
3882         hessian
3883         wronskian
3884         """
3885         if not isinstance(X, MatrixBase):
3886             X = self._new(X)
3887         # Both X and self can be a row or a column matrix, so we need to make
3888         # sure all valid combinations work, but everything else fails:
3889         if self.shape[0] == 1:
3890             m = self.shape[1]
3891         elif self.shape[1] == 1:
3892             m = self.shape[0]
3893         else:
3894             raise TypeError("self must be a row or a column matrix")
3895         if X.shape[0] == 1:
3896             n = X.shape[1]
3897         elif X.shape[1] == 1:
3898             n = X.shape[0]
3899         else:
3900             raise TypeError("X must be a row or a column matrix")
3901 
3902         # m is the number of functions and n is the number of variables
3903         # computing the Jacobian is now easy:
3904         return self._new(m, n, lambda j, i: self[j].diff(X[i]))
3905 
3906     def jordan_cell(self, eigenval, n):
3907         n = int(n)
3908         from sympy.matrices import MutableMatrix
3909         out = MutableMatrix.zeros(n)
3910         for i in range(n - 1):
3911             out[i, i] = eigenval
3912             out[i, i + 1] = 1
3913         out[n - 1, n - 1] = eigenval
3914         return type(self)(out)

3916     def jordan_cells(self, calc_transformation=True):
3917         r"""Return a list of Jordan cells of current matrix.
3918         This list shape Jordan matrix J.
3919 
3920         If calc_transformation is specified as False, then transformation P such that
3921 
3922               `J = P^{-1} \cdot M \cdot P`
3923 
3924         will not be calculated.
3925 
3926         Notes
3927         =====
3928 
3929         Calculation of transformation P is not implemented yet.
3930 
3931         Examples
3932         ========
3933 
3934         >>> from sympy import Matrix
3935         >>> m = Matrix(4, 4, [
3936         ...  6,  5, -2, -3,
3937         ... -3, -1,  3,  3,
3938         ...  2,  1, -2, -3,
3939         ... -1,  1,  5,  5])
3940 
3941         >>> P, Jcells = m.jordan_cells()
3942         >>> Jcells[0]
3943         Matrix([
3944         [2, 1],
3945         [0, 2]])
3946         >>> Jcells[1]
3947         Matrix([
3948         [2, 1],
3949         [0, 2]])
3950 
3951         See Also
3952         ========
3953 
3954         jordan_form
3955         """
3956         n = self.rows
3957         Jcells = []
3958         Pcols_new = []
3959         jordan_block_structures = self._jordan_block_structure()
3960         from sympy.matrices import MutableMatrix
3961 
3962         # Order according to default_sort_key, this makes sure the order is the same as in .diagonalize():
3963         for eigenval in (
3964         sorted(list(jordan_block_structures.keys()), key=default_sort_key)):
3965             l_jordan_chains = jordan_block_structures[eigenval]
3966             for s in reversed(sorted(
3967                     (l_jordan_chains).keys())):  # Start with the biggest block
3968                 s_chains = l_jordan_chains[s]
3969                 block = self.jordan_cell(eigenval, s)
3970                 number_of_s_chains = len(s_chains)
3971                 for i in range(0, number_of_s_chains):
3972                     Jcells.append(type(self)(block))
3973                     chain_vectors = s_chains[i]
3974                     lc = len(chain_vectors)
3975                     assert lc == s
3976                     for j in range(0, lc):
3977                         generalized_eigen_vector = chain_vectors[j]
3978                         Pcols_new.append(generalized_eigen_vector)
3979         P = MutableMatrix.zeros(n)
3980         for j in range(0, n):
3981             P[:, j] = Pcols_new[j]
3982 
3983         return type(self)(P), Jcells
3984 
3985     def jordan_form(self, calc_transformation=True):
3986         r"""Return Jordan form J of current matrix.
3987 
3988         Also the transformation P such that
3989 
3990             `J = P^{-1} \cdot M \cdot P`
3991 
3992         and the jordan blocks forming J
3993         will be calculated.
3994 
3995 
3996         Examples
3997         ========
3998 
3999         >>> from sympy import Matrix
4000         >>> m = Matrix([
4001         ...        [ 6,  5, -2, -3],
4002         ...        [-3, -1,  3,  3],
4003         ...        [ 2,  1, -2, -3],
4004         ...        [-1,  1,  5,  5]])
4005         >>> P, J = m.jordan_form()
4006         >>> J
4007         Matrix([
4008         [2, 1, 0, 0],
4009         [0, 2, 0, 0],
4010         [0, 0, 2, 1],
4011         [0, 0, 0, 2]])
4012 
4013         See Also
4014         ========
4015 
4016         jordan_cells
4017         """
4018         P, Jcells = self.jordan_cells()
4019         from sympy.matrices import diag
4020         J = diag(*Jcells)
4021         return P, type(self)(J)

4023     def key2bounds(self, keys):
4024         """Converts a key with potentially mixed types of keys (integer and slice)
4025         into a tuple of ranges and raises an error if any index is out of self's
4026         range.
4027 
4028         See Also
4029         ========
4030 
4031         key2ij
4032         """
4033 
4034         islice, jslice = [isinstance(k, slice) for k in keys]
4035         if islice:
4036             if not self.rows:
4037                 rlo = rhi = 0
4038             else:
4039                 rlo, rhi = keys[0].indices(self.rows)[:2]
4040         else:
4041             rlo = a2idx(keys[0], self.rows)
4042             rhi = rlo + 1
4043         if jslice:
4044             if not self.cols:
4045                 clo = chi = 0
4046             else:
4047                 clo, chi = keys[1].indices(self.cols)[:2]
4048         else:
4049             clo = a2idx(keys[1], self.cols)
4050             chi = clo + 1
4051         return rlo, rhi, clo, chi

4053     def key2ij(self, key):
4054         """Converts key into canonical form, converting integers or indexable
4055         items into valid integers for self's range or returning slices
4056         unchanged.
4057 
4058         See Also
4059         ========
4060 
4061         key2bounds
4062         """
4063         if is_sequence(key):
4064             if not len(key) == 2:
4065                 raise TypeError('key must be a sequence of length 2')
4066             return [a2idx(i, n) if not isinstance(i, slice) else i
4067                     for i, n in zip(key, self.shape)]
4068         elif isinstance(key, slice):
4069             return key.indices(len(self))[:2]
4070         else:
4071             return divmod(a2idx(key, len(self)), self.cols)

4073     def LDLdecomposition(self):
4074         """Returns the LDL Decomposition (L, D) of matrix A,
4075         such that L * D * L.T == A
4076         This method eliminates the use of square root.
4077         Further this ensures that all the diagonal entries of L are 1.
4078         A must be a square, symmetric, positive-definite
4079         and non-singular matrix.
4080 
4081         Examples
4082         ========
4083 
4084         >>> from sympy.matrices import Matrix, eye
4085         >>> A = Matrix(((25, 15, -5), (15, 18, 0), (-5, 0, 11)))
4086         >>> L, D = A.LDLdecomposition()
4087         >>> L
4088         Matrix([
4089         [   1,   0, 0],
4090         [ 3/5,   1, 0],
4091         [-1/5, 1/3, 1]])
4092         >>> D
4093         Matrix([
4094         [25, 0, 0],
4095         [ 0, 9, 0],
4096         [ 0, 0, 9]])
4097         >>> L * D * L.T * A.inv() == eye(A.rows)
4098         True
4099 
4100         See Also
4101         ========
4102 
4103         cholesky
4104         LUdecomposition
4105         QRdecomposition
4106         """
4107         if not self.is_square:
4108             raise NonSquareMatrixError("Matrix must be square.")
4109         if not self.is_symmetric():
4110             raise ValueError("Matrix must be symmetric.")
4111         return self._LDLdecomposition()

4113     def LDLsolve(self, rhs):
4114         """Solves Ax = B using LDL decomposition,
4115         for a general square and non-singular matrix.
4116 
4117         For a non-square matrix with rows > cols,
4118         the least squares solution is returned.
4119 
4120         Examples
4121         ========
4122 
4123         >>> from sympy.matrices import Matrix, eye
4124         >>> A = eye(2)*2
4125         >>> B = Matrix([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
4126         >>> A.LDLsolve(B) == B/2
4127         True
4128 
4129         See Also
4130         ========
4131 
4132         LDLdecomposition
4133         lower_triangular_solve
4134         upper_triangular_solve
4135         gauss_jordan_solve
4136         cholesky_solve
4137         diagonal_solve
4138         LUsolve
4139         QRsolve
4140         pinv_solve
4141         """
4142         if self.is_symmetric():
4143             L, D = self.LDLdecomposition()
4144         elif self.rows >= self.cols:
4145             L, D = (self.T * self).LDLdecomposition()
4146             rhs = self.T * rhs
4147         else:
4148             raise NotImplementedError('Under-determined System. '
4149                                       'Try M.gauss_jordan_solve(rhs)')
4150         Y = L._lower_triangular_solve(rhs)
4151         Z = D._diagonal_solve(Y)
4152         return (L.T)._upper_triangular_solve(Z)

4154     def left_eigenvects(self, **flags):
4155         """Returns left eigenvectors and eigenvalues.

4157         This function returns the list of triples (eigenval, multiplicity,
4158         basis) for the left eigenvectors. Options are the same as for
4159         eigenvects(), i.e. the ``**flags`` arguments gets passed directly to
4160         eigenvects().

4169         [-1],
4170         [ 1],
4171         [ 0]])]), (0, 1, [Matrix([
4172         [ 0],
4173         [-1],
4174         [ 1]])]), (2, 1, [Matrix([
4175         [2/3],
4176         [1/3],

4239     def LUdecomposition(self, iszerofunc=_iszero):
4240         """Returns the decomposition LU and the row swaps p.
4241 
4242         Examples
4243         ========
4244 
4245         >>> from sympy import Matrix
4246         >>> a = Matrix([[4, 3], [6, 3]])
4247         >>> L, U, _ = a.LUdecomposition()
4248         >>> L
4249         Matrix([
4250         [  1, 0],
4251         [3/2, 1]])
4252         >>> U
4253         Matrix([
4254         [4,    3],
4255         [0, -3/2]])
4256 
4257         See Also
4258         ========
4259 
4260         cholesky
4261         LDLdecomposition
4262         QRdecomposition
4263         LUdecomposition_Simple
4264         LUdecompositionFF
4265         LUsolve
4266         """
4267         combined, p = self.LUdecomposition_Simple(iszerofunc=_iszero)
4268         L = self.zeros(self.rows)
4269         U = self.zeros(self.rows)
4270         for i in range(self.rows):
4271             for j in range(self.rows):
4272                 if i > j:
4273                     L[i, j] = combined[i, j]
4274                 else:
4275                     if i == j:
4276                         L[i, i] = 1
4277                     U[i, j] = combined[i, j]
4278         return L, U, p
4279 
4280     def LUdecomposition_Simple(self, iszerofunc=_iszero):
4281         """Returns A comprised of L, U (L's diag entries are 1) and
4282         p which is the list of the row swaps (in order).
4283 
4284         See Also
4285         ========
4286 
4287         LUdecomposition
4288         LUdecompositionFF
4289         LUsolve
4290         """
4291         if not self.is_square:
4292             raise NonSquareMatrixError(
4293                 "A Matrix must be square to apply LUdecomposition_Simple().")
4294         n = self.rows
4295         A = self.as_mutable()
4296         p = []
4297         # factorization
4298         for j in range(n):
4299             for i in range(j):
4300                 for k in range(i):
4301                     A[i, j] = A[i, j] - A[i, k] * A[k, j]
4302             pivot = -1
4303             for i in range(j, n):
4304                 for k in range(j):
4305                     A[i, j] = A[i, j] - A[i, k] * A[k, j]
4306                 # find the first non-zero pivot, includes any expression
4307                 if pivot == -1 and not iszerofunc(A[i, j]):
4308                     pivot = i
4309             if pivot < 0:
4310                 # this result is based on iszerofunc's analysis of the possible pivots, so even though
4311                 # the element may not be strictly zero, the supplied iszerofunc's evaluation gave True
4312                 raise ValueError("No nonzero pivot found; inversion failed.")
4313             if pivot != j:  # row must be swapped
4314                 A.row_swap(pivot, j)
4315                 p.append([pivot, j])
4316             scale = 1 / A[j, j]
4317             for i in range(j + 1, n):
4318                 A[i, j] = A[i, j] * scale
4319         return A, p
4320 
4321     def LUdecompositionFF(self):
4322         """Compute a fraction-free LU decomposition.
4323 
4324         Returns 4 matrices P, L, D, U such that PA = L D**-1 U.
4325         If the elements of the matrix belong to some integral domain I, then all
4326         elements of L, D and U are guaranteed to belong to I.
4327 
4328         **Reference**
4329             - W. Zhou & D.J. Jeffrey, "Fraction-free matrix factors: new forms
4330               for LU and QR factors". Frontiers in Computer Science in China,
4331               Vol 2, no. 1, pp. 67-80, 2008.
4332 
4333         See Also
4334         ========
4335 
4336         LUdecomposition
4337         LUdecomposition_Simple
4338         LUsolve
4339         """
4340         from sympy.matrices import SparseMatrix
4341         zeros = SparseMatrix.zeros
4342         eye = SparseMatrix.eye
4343 
4344         n, m = self.rows, self.cols
4345         U, L, P = self.as_mutable(), eye(n), eye(n)
4346         DD = zeros(n, n)
4347         oldpivot = 1
4348 
4349         for k in range(n - 1):
4350             if U[k, k] == 0:
4351                 for kpivot in range(k + 1, n):
4352                     if U[kpivot, k]:
4353                         break
4354                 else:
4355                     raise ValueError("Matrix is not full rank")
4356                 U[k, k:], U[kpivot, k:] = U[kpivot, k:], U[k, k:]
4357                 L[k, :k], L[kpivot, :k] = L[kpivot, :k], L[k, :k]
4358                 P[k, :], P[kpivot, :] = P[kpivot, :], P[k, :]
4359             L[k, k] = Ukk = U[k, k]
4360             DD[k, k] = oldpivot * Ukk
4361             for i in range(k + 1, n):
4362                 L[i, k] = Uik = U[i, k]
4363                 for j in range(k + 1, m):
4364                     U[i, j] = (Ukk * U[i, j] - U[k, j] * Uik) / oldpivot
4365                 U[i, k] = 0
4366             oldpivot = Ukk
4367         DD[n - 1, n - 1] = oldpivot
4368         return P, L, DD, U
4369 
4370     def LUsolve(self, rhs, iszerofunc=_iszero):
4371         """Solve the linear system Ax = rhs for x where A = self.
4372 
4373         This is for symbolic matrices, for real or complex ones use
4374         mpmath.lu_solve or mpmath.qr_solve.
4375 
4376         See Also
4377         ========
4378 
4379         lower_triangular_solve
4380         upper_triangular_solve
4381         gauss_jordan_solve
4382         cholesky_solve
4383         diagonal_solve
4384         LDLsolve
4385         QRsolve
4386         pinv_solve
4387         LUdecomposition
4388         """
4389         if rhs.rows != self.rows:
4390             raise ShapeError(
4391                 "`self` and `rhs` must have the same number of rows.")
4392 
4393         A, perm = self.LUdecomposition_Simple(iszerofunc=_iszero)
4394         n = self.rows
4395         b = rhs.permuteFwd(perm).as_mutable()
4396         # forward substitution, all diag entries are scaled to 1
4397         for i in range(n):
4398             for j in range(i):
4399                 scale = A[i, j]
4400                 b.zip_row_op(i, j, lambda x, y: x - y * scale)
4401         # backward substitution
4402         for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
4403             for j in range(i + 1, n):
4404                 scale = A[i, j]
4405                 b.zip_row_op(i, j, lambda x, y: x - y * scale)
4406             scale = A[i, i]
4407             b.row_op(i, lambda x, _: x / scale)
4408         return rhs.__class__(b)

4465         >>> from sympy import Matrix, Symbol, trigsimp, cos, sin, oo
4466         >>> x = Symbol('x', real=True)
4467         >>> v = Matrix([cos(x), sin(x)])
4468         >>> trigsimp( v.norm() )
4469         1
4470         >>> v.norm(10)
4471         (sin(x)**10 + cos(x)**10)**(1/10)
4472         >>> A = Matrix([[1, 1], [1, 1]])
4473         >>> A.norm(2)# Spectral norm (max of |Ax|/|x| under 2-vector-norm)
4474         2
4475         >>> A.norm(-2) # Inverse spectral norm (smallest singular value)
4476         0
4477         >>> A.norm() # Frobenius Norm
4478         2
4479         >>> Matrix([1, -2]).norm(oo)
4480         2
4481         >>> Matrix([-1, 2]).norm(-oo)
4482         1
4483 
4484         See Also
4485         ========
4486 
4487         normalized
4488         """
4489         # Row or Column Vector Norms
4490         vals = list(self.values()) or [0]
4491         if self.rows == 1 or self.cols == 1:
4492             if ord == 2 or ord is None:  # Common case sqrt(<x, x>)
4493                 return sqrt(Add(*(abs(i) ** 2 for i in vals)))
4494 
4495             elif ord == 1:  # sum(abs(x))
4496                 return Add(*(abs(i) for i in vals))
4497 
4498             elif ord == S.Infinity:  # max(abs(x))
4499                 return Max(*[abs(i) for i in vals])
4500 
4501             elif ord == S.NegativeInfinity:  # min(abs(x))
4502                 return Min(*[abs(i) for i in vals])
4503 
4504             # Otherwise generalize the 2-norm, Sum(x_i**ord)**(1/ord)
4505             # Note that while useful this is not mathematically a norm
4506             try:
4507                 return Pow(Add(*(abs(i) ** ord for i in vals)), S(1) / ord)
4508             except (NotImplementedError, TypeError):
4509                 raise ValueError("Expected order to be Number, Symbol, oo")
4510 
4511         # Matrix Norms
4512         else:
4513             if ord == 2:  # Spectral Norm
4514                 # Maximum singular value
4515                 return Max(*self.singular_values())
4516 
4517             elif ord == -2:
4518                 # Minimum singular value
4519                 return Min(*self.singular_values())
4520 
4521             elif (ord is None or isinstance(ord,
4522                                             string_types) and ord.lower() in
4523                 ['f', 'fro', 'frobenius', 'vector']):
4524                 # Reshape as vector and send back to norm function
4525                 return self.vec().norm(ord=2)
4526 
4527             else:
4528                 raise NotImplementedError("Matrix Norms under development")

4557             simplify, FunctionType) else _simplify

4574                 for j in range(i + 1, self.cols):

4578                         v = simpfunc(v)

4583                                 "Could not compute the nullspace of `self`.")

4635     def pinv_solve(self, B, arbitrary_matrix=None):
4636         """Solve Ax = B using the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse.
4637 
4638         There may be zero, one, or infinite solutions.  If one solution
4639         exists, it will be returned.  If infinite solutions exist, one will
4640         be returned based on the value of arbitrary_matrix.  If no solutions
4641         exist, the least-squares solution is returned.
4642 
4643         Parameters
4644         ==========
4645 
4646         B : Matrix
4647             The right hand side of the equation to be solved for.  Must have
4648             the same number of rows as matrix A.
4649         arbitrary_matrix : Matrix
4650             If the system is underdetermined (e.g. A has more columns than
4651             rows), infinite solutions are possible, in terms of an arbitrary
4652             matrix.  This parameter may be set to a specific matrix to use
4653             for that purpose; if so, it must be the same shape as x, with as
4654             many rows as matrix A has columns, and as many columns as matrix
4655             B.  If left as None, an appropriate matrix containing dummy
4656             symbols in the form of ``wn_m`` will be used, with n and m being
4657             row and column position of each symbol.
4658 
4659         Returns
4660         =======
4661 
4662         x : Matrix
4663             The matrix that will satisfy Ax = B.  Will have as many rows as
4664             matrix A has columns, and as many columns as matrix B.
4665 
4666         Examples
4667         ========
4668 
4669         >>> from sympy import Matrix
4670         >>> A = Matrix([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
4671         >>> B = Matrix([7, 8])
4672         >>> A.pinv_solve(B)
4673         Matrix([
4674         [ _w0_0/6 - _w1_0/3 + _w2_0/6 - 55/18],
4675         [-_w0_0/3 + 2*_w1_0/3 - _w2_0/3 + 1/9],
4676         [ _w0_0/6 - _w1_0/3 + _w2_0/6 + 59/18]])
4677         >>> A.pinv_solve(B, arbitrary_matrix=Matrix([0, 0, 0]))
4678         Matrix([
4679         [-55/18],
4680         [   1/9],
4681         [ 59/18]])
4682 
4683         See Also
4684         ========
4685 
4686         lower_triangular_solve
4687         upper_triangular_solve
4688         gauss_jordan_solve
4689         cholesky_solve
4690         diagonal_solve
4691         LDLsolve
4692         LUsolve
4693         QRsolve
4694         pinv
4695 
4696         Notes
4697         =====
4698 
4699         This may return either exact solutions or least squares solutions.
4700         To determine which, check ``A * A.pinv() * B == B``.  It will be
4701         True if exact solutions exist, and False if only a least-squares
4702         solution exists.  Be aware that the left hand side of that equation
4703         may need to be simplified to correctly compare to the right hand
4704         side.
4705 
4706         References
4707         ==========
4708 
4709         .. [1] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moore-Penrose_pseudoinverse#Obtaining_all_solutions_of_a_linear_system
4710 
4711         """
4712         from sympy.matrices import eye
4713         A = self
4714         A_pinv = self.pinv()
4715         if arbitrary_matrix is None:
4716             rows, cols = A.cols, B.cols
4717             w = symbols('w:{0}_:{1}'.format(rows, cols), cls=Dummy)
4718             arbitrary_matrix = self.__class__(cols, rows, w).T
4719         return A_pinv * B + (eye(A.cols) - A_pinv * A) * arbitrary_matrix
4720 
4721     def pinv(self):
4722         """Calculate the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of the matrix.
4723 
4724         The Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse exists and is unique for any matrix.
4725         If the matrix is invertible, the pseudoinverse is the same as the
4726         inverse.
4727 
4728         Examples
4729         ========
4730 
4731         >>> from sympy import Matrix
4732         >>> Matrix([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]).pinv()
4733         Matrix([
4734         [-17/18,  4/9],
4735         [  -1/9,  1/9],
4736         [ 13/18, -2/9]])
4737 
4738         See Also
4739         ========
4740 
4741         inv
4742         pinv_solve
4743 
4744         References
4745         ==========
4746 
4747         .. [1] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moore-Penrose_pseudoinverse
4748 
4749         """
4750         A = self
4751         AH = self.H
4752         # Trivial case: pseudoinverse of all-zero matrix is its transpose.
4753         if A.is_zero:
4754             return AH
4755         try:
4756             if self.rows >= self.cols:
4757                 return (AH * A).inv() * AH
4758             else:
4759                 return AH * (A * AH).inv()
4760         except ValueError:
4761             # Matrix is not full rank, so A*AH cannot be inverted.
4762             raise NotImplementedError('Rank-deficient matrices are not yet '
4763                                       'supported.')
4764
